title: Stability and Phase Margin
intro: A feedback system is stable if its poles are in the left half plane. The Bode plot of the loop gain tells you how close it is to the edge.

blocks.text: A feedback loop oscillates when at some frequency the loop gain has magnitude 1 and phase -180 degrees, so that negative feedback becomes positive. A stable design keeps |A*beta| below 1 whenever the phase reaches -180 degrees.

items: Phase margin (PM): 180 degrees + phase(A*beta) at the gain crossover. PM of 45 degrees is the bare minimum; 60 degrees is a common target.
Gain margin: how much |A*beta| can rise at the -180 degree frequency before it reaches 1.
A low PM shows up as peaking in the closed-loop frequency response and ringing in the step response.

blocks.alt: Two stacked Bode plots of a loop gain with two poles. The top plot shows the magnitude falling from 60 dB, crossing 0 dB near 1 MHz. The bottom plot shows the phase falling toward minus 180 degrees. A vertical dotted line links the 0 dB crossing to the phase curve, and an arrow marks the phase margin, the gap between the phase at that frequency and minus 180 degrees, about 55 degrees.
blocks.caption: The phase margin is read at the unity-gain frequency, as the distance of the phase from -180 degrees.

widget.title: Step response of a feedback amplifier with two poles

blocks.text: The slider sets the second pole relative to the loop's unity-gain frequency. At 1 the phase margin is 45 degrees, with substantial overshoot; at 2 it is 63 degrees and the response is well damped; at 0.5 it is 27 degrees and rings badly.

blocks.title: Phase margin of a two-pole loop
blocks.text: A loop has a dominant pole and a second pole at twice the unity-gain frequency. Find the phase margin.
solution: The first pole gives -90 degrees at crossover (well above it). The second pole gives -arctan(wu/wp2) = -arctan(0.5) = -26.6 degrees.

blocks.title: Choosing the second pole
blocks.text: What second-pole location gives a phase margin of 45 degrees?
solution: PM = 90 - arctan(wu/wp2) = 45 requires arctan(wu/wp2) = 45 degrees, so wp2 = wu.
